1	# Sentence patterns
2	
3	A catalog of recurring sentence-level patterns and their fixes, plus the within-paragraph cohesion mechanics that make prose flow. Load this when the sentence-level cohesion lens in SKILL.md names a flow or pattern problem and a concrete diagnosis is useful for the change rationale.
4	
5	The theory behind the cohesion moves (Williams's old-new flow, Gopen and Swan's reader-expectation positions) lives in `references/principles.md`; this file is the operational version. The AI-tell list and banned-transition policy live in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`, not here.
6	
7	## Cohesion within the paragraph
8	
9	The patterns below fix single sentences; these three moves fix how consecutive sentences hold together. (`references/principles.md` gives the underlying theory.)
10	
11	**The given-new chain.** Place what the reader already knows at the start of a sentence and the new information at the end; the new information of one sentence becomes the given information of the next, pulling the reader forward. The common failure is front-loading a sentence with a new technical term before the reader has an anchor.
12	
13	| Before | After |
14	|---|---|
15	| Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors were computed. The HC3 variant was used for its small-sample properties. | We computed standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity. Among the variants, HC3 performs best in small samples, so we used it. |
16	
17	Diagnostic: for each sentence, ask whether it opens on something the previous sentence established. Build transitions from this chain (end a sentence on the term the next will pick up) rather than from a transition word bolted on top.
18	
19	**Topic strings.** Within a paragraph, the subjects of consecutive sentences should form a coherent set. If the subjects jump around (the data, the model, the result, the field), the reader reorients every sentence; if they stay related (the model, its parameters, its predictions, its limits), the reader stays oriented. Diagnostic: name the subject of every sentence in the paragraph. If you cannot do it in one breath, the topic string is broken.
20	
21	**Sentence-length variety.** A run of uniform-length sentences reads mechanically, and uniform length is itself an AI tell. Vary the rhythm: land a point with a short sentence after a long one, build out a complex idea with a long sentence after several short ones. This is not mechanical alternation; it means writing for the ear and reading the result aloud.
22	
23	**Paragraph-shape variety.** The paragraph-scale version of the same tell, and the stronger one. When every paragraph runs the same mold (a topic claim, three evenly weighted supporting sentences, then a "Taken together" or "In summary" restatement of the opener), the section reads mechanically even with every banned word gone, because the shape repeats. Vary it: let some paragraphs be two sentences, let the load-bearing one build across several, and cut the closing restatement when the paragraph already landed its point (a recap that only re-states the opener is the say-it-once echo, `references/subtraction.md`). This is the structural sibling of the sentence-length tell above and of "List rhythm" in `references/reader-pleasure.md`.
24	
25	## Nominalizations
26	
27	A nominalization is a noun made from a verb or adjective. Nominalizations are not bad in themselves; they are useful when the action is the topic. They become a problem when they bury the action of a sentence behind a weak verb.
28	
29	**Pattern:** Subject + form of "to be" or "conduct" or "perform" or "make" or "have" + nominalization.
30	
31	| Before | After |
32	|---|---|
33	| We performed an analysis of the data. | We analyzed the data. |
34	| There is a need for further investigation. | We need to investigate further. |
35	| A comparison was made between A and B. | We compared A and B. |
36	| The contribution of this paper is the development of a new method. | This paper develops a new method. |
37	| Our hope is that future work will provide a resolution to this issue. | We hope future work resolves this. |
38	
39	Diagnostic: scan for words ending in *-tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ity, -ness* paired with weak verbs. If the noun names an action and the verb is doing no work, fold the action into the verb.
40	
41	Exception: when the nominalization names the topic and the action is genuinely secondary, leave it. "Our analysis of the corpus revealed three patterns" is fine; "analysis" is the topic.
42	
43	## Throat-clearing openings
44	
45	Throat-clearing is the academic habit of starting sentences with phrases that announce what is about to happen rather than saying it.
46	
47	| Throat-clearing | Direct |
48	|---|---|
49	| It is important to note that the effect is small. | The effect is small. |
50	| It should be emphasized that participants varied widely. | Participants varied widely. |
51	| One thing to keep in mind is that the data are skewed. | The data are skewed. |
52	| What we want to argue here is that X causes Y. | X causes Y. |
53	| It is worth pointing out that prior work has neglected this. | Prior work has neglected this. |
54	
55	Diagnostic: if you can delete the opening clause and the sentence still says what it means, delete it. The opening clause was telling the reader what was about to happen rather than telling them what is so.
56	
57	## Existential and expletive constructions
58	
59	"There is", "there are", "it is", "it was" used as dummy subjects. They are not wrong, but they put the topic in the wrong place.
60	
61	| Before | After |
62	|---|---|
63	| There are several reasons that motivate this work. | Several reasons motivate this work. |
64	| It is the case that the model overfits on small datasets. | The model overfits on small datasets. |
65	| There exists a tradeoff between recall and precision. | Recall and precision trade off against each other. |
66	| It is clear that further work is needed. | (Delete; if it is clear, you do not need to say so.) |
67	
68	Diagnostic: find "there is", "there are", "there exists", "it is", "it was". For each, ask whether the real topic is being introduced after the dummy subject. If so, restructure.
69	
70	Exception: "there" constructions are useful when the existence itself is the point ("There are exactly three solutions to this equation"). Use them deliberately.
71	
72	## The emphatic cleft habit
73	
74	An it-cleft ("It is X that Y") or a wh-cleft ("What Y does is X") splits a plain clause to spotlight one element. Used once for a genuine contrast it earns its place; LLMs reach for it by default, and it pushes the real subject rightward, delaying the verb the way "Misplaced stress" and "The interrupted clause" do. Unlike the expletive "it is" above, the fix is not deletion: the cleft encodes contrastive focus, so recast to a plain subject-verb only when that focus is not real.
75	
76	| Before | After |
77	|---|---|
78	| It is the interaction between prompt length and model size that drives the effect. | The interaction between prompt length and model size drives the effect. |
79	| What the ablation shows is that the gain comes from the reranker. | The ablation shows that the gain comes from the reranker. |
80	
81	Diagnostic: for each "It is/was X that/who ..." and "What ... is/does ...", ask whether the sentence is correcting a specific wrong alternative the reader would otherwise credit. If it is, keep the cleft; the focus is doing work. If it is emphasis by default, unfold it to subject-verb.
82	
83	## Noun pile-ups
84	
85	A noun pile-up is three or more nouns adjacent, where the reader has to guess which modifies which.
86	
87	| Before | After |
88	|---|---|
89	| User behavior analysis framework design | Design of a framework for analyzing user behavior |
90	| Survey response quality measurement instrument | Instrument for measuring the quality of survey responses |
91	| Algorithm performance evaluation methodology | Methodology for evaluating algorithm performance |
92	
93	Diagnostic: count adjacent nouns. Two is usually fine. Three is suspicious. Four is almost always wrong. Fix by breaking the pile with prepositions ("of", "for", "in", "with"). Watch the mirror-image failure: too many such prepositional phrases in a row hold the verb off, which is the prepositional-chain variant under `The interrupted clause` below.
94	
95	## Hedge stacking
96	
97	Hedges (modal verbs and adverbs that qualify a claim) are useful for honesty. Stacked, they become evasive.
98	
99	| Before | After |
100	|---|---|
101	| This may possibly suggest that perhaps X causes Y. | This suggests X may cause Y. |
102	| It could be argued that one might consider the possibility that... | One possibility: ... |
103	| The results seem to potentially indicate a tendency toward... | The results suggest a tendency toward... |
104	
105	Rule: one hedge per claim, maximum; a claim too uncertain to make with a single hedge should not be made, and a claim solid enough to make takes one hedge or none. Exception: a hedge that marks genuine calibration or scope ("on the held-out set", "correlational", a qualifier that bounds the claim to what the evidence bears) is content, not filler; keep it, and count it as the claim's one hedge rather than stripping it (see the qualifier-is-content rule in SKILL.md and `references/subtraction.md`).
106	
107	## Overclaiming
108	
109	The opposite failure: language stronger than the evidence supports. Where hedge-stacking dilutes a sound claim, overclaiming inflates a weak one. Both are miscalibration; the editor flags the change rather than rewriting the claim, because only the author knows what the evidence will bear.
110	
111	| Before | After (flag for the author) |
112	|---|---|
113	| X causes Y. | X is associated with Y. (Is the design causal, or correlational?) |
114	| Our method proves that ... | Our results are consistent with ... (Does the evidence prove, or support?) |
115	| This holds in all settings. | This holds on the three datasets we tested. (Was it tested beyond these?) |
116	| The model is robust. | The model's accuracy stays within 2 points under perturbation P. (Robust to what?) |
117	
118	Diagnostic: for each strong verb ("causes", "proves", "demonstrates", "establishes", "guarantees") and each universal ("all", "always", "any", "every"), check that the evidence in the section reaches that far. If it does not, surface the gap as an Author question rather than silently weakening the claim.
119	
120	## Misplaced stress
121	
122	The end of an English sentence carries emphasis. When the important word lands mid-sentence and trivia lands at the end, the sentence reads backwards.
123	
124	| Before | After |
125	|---|---|
126	| Performance dropped by 40% in the ablation experiment, as we found. | The ablation dropped performance by 40%. |
127	| The framework, which we describe in detail in Section 3, achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks. | The framework achieves state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks; we describe it in Section 3. |
128	| Annotators agreed on 86% of items, after deliberation, which is high. | After deliberation, annotators agreed on 86% of items, a high rate. |
129	
130	Diagnostic: for each sentence, identify the most important word. Check whether it is in the stress position. If not, restructure.
131	
132	## The buried thesis
133	
134	The sentence that carries a passage's main point should be the easiest to read, not the hardest. The failure is the reverse: the takeaway arrives as the most clause-laden sentence in the paragraph, so the reader decodes syntax exactly where they most need the point to land clean. Fix by putting a character in the subject, the claim in an active verb, and any qualification in a following sentence rather than a nested clause.
135	
136	| Before | After |
137	|---|---|
138	| On this evidence the interface relocates the visible work of querying rather than demonstrably removing work: for our SQL-literate participants a verification burden survives the switch to natural language, and an NLIDB that hides the generated SQL would remove the very step these users relied on to trust the answer. | The interface moves the visible work of querying rather than demonstrably removing it. Our SQL-literate participants still had to verify the generated SQL, and an NLIDB that hid it would remove the very step they relied on to trust the answer. |
139	| The observation that performance degrades under distribution shift, which prior work had attributed to representation collapse, is shown by our ablations to instead follow from optimizer state. | Our ablations trace the performance drop under distribution shift to optimizer state, not the representation collapse prior work blamed. |
140	
141	Diagnostic: find the sentence stating the paragraph's main claim. If it is the longest or most deeply nested sentence in the paragraph, split it: lead with the claim in plain subject-verb-object order, and demote the qualifications to following sentences. Plainness is a change in syntax, not in strength: carry the evidential qualifiers and hedges through unchanged (here "visible" and "demonstrably", which bound the claim to what the study shows), or the plainer sentence asserts more than the original. This is the sentence-level form of "The load-bearing sentence is the plainest" in `references/altitude.md`.
142	
143	## The interrupted clause
144	
145	A clause keeps the reader in suspense until its core resolves: a subject needs its verb, a linking verb needs its complement, a verb needs its object, an object needs its complement, and so on for any element and the word that completes it. When an interrupting constituent opens up in one of those gaps, the reader has to hold an unfinished clause in working memory (the four-chunk budget in `references/principles.md`) until the sentence finally closes. The interrupter can be any kind of syntactic unit set into the gap: an appositive ("that question, calibration, open"), a parenthetical, a non-restrictive relative clause ("The interface, which relocates the visible work of querying, produced ..."), or an interposed adverbial, often stacked with a connective ("The results, however, when compared against the baseline, suggest ..."). What matters is the interrupter's position, in a gap the core has not yet closed, not its grammatical type; the type only tells you where the fix's trailing material should reattach. A sentence can trip this way while passing every other check: correct terminology, a topic sentence up front, no banned tell, a payoff at the end. The fix closes the gap so the core resolves without interruption: bring the stranded completing word up to the element it completes, or move the interrupting material to a trailing clause or its own sentence, always carrying that material through unchanged.
146	
147	| Before | After | Gap closed |
148	|---|---|---|
149	| Our data leave that question, calibration, open. | Our data leave open the question of calibration. | object and complement (`leave ... open`) |
150	| Those conditions, team literacy, schema design, and task framing, are the axes most likely to vary. | Those conditions are the axes most likely to vary: team literacy, schema design, and task framing. | subject and verb (`conditions ... are`) |
151	| One conjecture, untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population, is that the models have matured. | One conjecture is that the models have matured. That conjecture is untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population. | subject and verb (`conjecture ... is`) |
152	| The interface, which relocates rather than removes the visible work of querying, produced no reduction in task time. | The interface produced no reduction in task time. It relocates the visible work of querying rather than removing it. | subject and verb (`interface ... produced`); non-restrictive relative clause |
153	| The results, however, when compared against the baseline reported in prior work, suggest a smaller effect. | Compared against the baseline reported in prior work, however, the results suggest a smaller effect. | subject and verb (`results ... suggest`); interposed adverbial |
154	
155	Note how each rewrite keeps the interrupting words verbatim ("calibration"; "untestable across studies that differ in task, interface, and population"; "which relocates rather than removes the visible work of querying") and only changes where they sit, never what they claim. The gap can close either way: the first brings the stranded complement "open" up to the verb and leaves "calibration" where it was, while the others move the interrupting material to the end or the front. When a trailing phrase would dangle (in the third, "untestable ..." at the end would read as modifying "the models have matured" rather than "conjecture"), give it its own sentence with an explicit referent instead. The last two rows show the widening: a non-restrictive relative clause and an interposed adverbial are neither appositive nor parenthetical, but they open in the same subject-verb gap and take the same fix.
156	
157	### Machine-generated variants
158	
159	These three are the specifically LLM-generated forms of the interrupted clause. Each composes with a rule stated elsewhere, and each carries content that must move rather than die.
160	
161	**The first-mention gloss.** The model glosses a term at first mention by setting the definition into the subject-verb gap; this is the strongest LLM instance of the shape. "Retrieval-augmented generation, an architecture that retrieves passages before generating, underperformed the fine-tuned baseline." The gloss is real content, so it moves rather than dies: "Retrieval-augmented generation underperformed the fine-tuned baseline. The architecture retrieves passages before generating." This composes with the first-mention-versus-full-statement rule in `references/precision-budget.md`: the claim runs clean at first mention, and the definition lands once, in its own sentence or wherever the term is established.
162	
163	**The prepositional chain that holds off the verb.** No set-off constituent at all, but a chain of prepositional phrases stretches the subject and its verb apart. "The effect of the intervention on retention among first-year students in the treatment arm was small." The subject core ("The effect") and its verb ("was") sit eight words apart. Front the qualifying phrases: "Among first-year students in the treatment arm, the intervention had a small effect on retention." This is the mirror image of a noun pile-up (`Noun pile-ups` above): there, stacked nouns collapse the modifiers together; here, the prepositions that would break such a pile-up instead stretch the subject-verb gap. The diagnostic below catches both, because both leave the verb waiting.
164	
165	**The split correlative.** An embedded clause holds a correlative pair ("not only ... but also", "either ... or", "both ... and") open across the interruption. "The system not only reduces grading time, which was the original motivation, but also improves consistency." Close the correlative so its two halves sit together and demote the interrupter: "The system not only reduces grading time but also improves consistency. Reducing grading time was the original motivation." This ties to the "not only ... but also more than once in a section" tell in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`: if closing the correlative leaves a second one nearby, recast rather than repeat.
166	
167	Diagnostic: for each sentence, trace the core of every clause it contains, embedded clauses included, and check that no interrupting constituent sits in a gap the core has not yet closed, whatever its grammatical type, and that no chain of modifiers holds a verb out of reach. Length is not the test: a single interrupting word counts when it holds the completing word out of reach (above, the lone "calibration" delays "open"), while a brief parenthetical the reader resolves without losing the core can stay. Carry the interrupting material through unchanged, since a scope or calibration qualifier is content (the qualifier-is-content rule in `references/subtraction.md`). "The buried thesis" above is this pattern applied to a paragraph's main-claim sentence; both share the plainness principle of "The load-bearing sentence is the plainest" in `references/altitude.md`.
168	
169	## The left-branching preamble
170	
171	A sibling of the interrupted clause, with the same working-memory cost (`references/principles.md`) but a different fix. Here the material sits before the core opens, not inside it: a stack of subordinate clauses runs ahead of the main subject and verb, so the reader carries the preamble unresolved until the core finally arrives. "Because the annotators disagreed on the hard cases, and given that the training set over-represents them, the model fails to generalize." The gap-closing fix does not apply, because no gap has opened yet; the core has not started. Instead, front the core and demote the preamble to a trailing clause or a following sentence: "The model fails to generalize: the annotators disagreed on the hard cases, and the training set over-represents them." As with the interrupted clause, the demoted material carries through unchanged; only its position moves. A short single preamble ("Because X, the model fails") is fine, the way a brief parenthetical is; the tell is the stack, two or more subordinate clauses held open before the core.
172	
173	Diagnostic: for each sentence, find where the main subject and verb begin. If two or more subordinate or participial clauses precede them, front the core and trail the rest. One leading clause is rhythm; a stack is a preamble. This shares the stress principle of "Misplaced stress" above (the core belongs where the reader can act on it) and the plainness of "The buried thesis".
174	
175	## Wordiness compounds
176	
177	Common multi-word phrases that have shorter equivalents. Cutting them is the easiest revision pass.
178	
179	| Before | After |
180	|---|---|
181	| in order to | to |
182	| due to the fact that | because |
183	| at this point in time | now |
184	| a large number of | many |
185	| a small number of | few |
186	| in spite of the fact that | although |
187	| with the exception of | except |
188	| in the event that | if |
189	| for the purpose of | for, to |
190	| in close proximity to | near |
191	| has the ability to | can |
192	| is able to | can |
193	| make use of | use |
194	| in the case of | for, with |
195	| it is often the case that | often |
196	| the majority of | most |
197	| in addition to the fact that | besides |
198	| the fact that | (recast: "due to the fact that" -> "because"; "aware of the fact that" -> "aware that") |
199	| in terms of | (name the dimension, or delete) |
200	| a number of | several, many |
201	| the way in which | how |
202	| serves to [verb] | [verb] ("serves to clarify" -> "clarifies") |
203	
204	These are search-and-replace targets. Run them first; they almost always shorten without loss.
205	
206	## Vague abstractions
207	
208	Abstract nouns that hide the underlying concrete claim. Common offenders: "aspects", "factors", "issues", "considerations", "elements", "things", "approaches".
209	
210	| Before | After |
211	|---|---|
212	| Several factors influence the result. | Three things influence the result: A, B, and C. |
213	| Various aspects of the problem need consideration. | (Name the aspects.) |
214	| There are issues with the methodology. | (Name the issues.) |
215	| Different approaches have been proposed. | (Name them, or summarize their shared logic.) |
216	
217	Diagnostic: when you see one of these abstract nouns, ask what concrete content it stands for. If you cannot answer, the writer probably could not either. Flag as an author question.
218	
219	## Misused connectives
220	
221	Common errors with logical connectives that obscure argument structure.
222	
223	- **"However"** signals contrast. If the next sentence does not contrast with the prior one, do not use it.
224	- **"Thus", "therefore", "hence"** signal logical consequence. If the next sentence does not follow logically, do not use them.
225	- **"Indeed"** signals confirming evidence. It is overused as a generic intensifier.
226	- **"While"** is ambiguous between "during" and "although". Prefer "although" or "whereas" for the contrastive meaning, especially in academic prose.
227	
228	Note: the banned-transition list in `references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md` is the canonical source. The above are about misuse of allowed connectives, not bans.
229	
230	## Accumulation instead of argument
231	
232	Banning "Furthermore", "Moreover", and "Additionally" (`references/ai-tells-to-avoid.md`) removes the word, not the habit under it: claims strung together as coordinate equals when one actually causes, enables, or qualifies the next. Delete the connective and the flat list is still there.
233	
234	| Before | After |
235	|---|---|
236	| The baseline fails on rare classes. Our method reweights them. Additionally, accuracy improves. | The baseline fails on rare classes, so our method reweights them; accuracy improves as a result. |
237	| Annotators disagreed on the hard cases. The training set over-represents them. Moreover, the model inherits the noise. | Because annotators disagreed on the hard cases that the training set over-represents, the model inherits the noise. |
238	
239	Diagnostic: for a run of same-shaped declaratives joined by additive connectives or by nothing, ask what relation actually holds between them: does one cause, enable, qualify, or contrast with the next? Name that relation with the connective that fits (because, so, but, despite). The license comes from the author's own material: a juxtaposition that already implies the relation may be made explicit, but a relation the text does not support is new substance, so flag it in `Author questions` rather than inventing it. When the items are genuinely independent, an explicit list is more honest than additive glue. The test is whether reordering the sentences changes the meaning; if it does not, they are being accumulated, not argued. See "List rhythm" in `references/reader-pleasure.md`; for why a draft defaults to this equal-weight mold, see "Why the defensive draft reads flat" in `references/precision-budget.md`.
240	
241	## Dangling references
242	
243	Pronouns and definite articles that point at things the reader cannot identify.
244	
245	| Before | After |
246	|---|---|
247	| This is a problem for downstream applications. | This ambiguity is a problem for downstream applications. |
248	| The result was unexpected. | The accuracy result was unexpected. |
249	| It suggests a different mechanism. | The 40% drop suggests a different mechanism. |
250	
251	The "this + noun" rule: when "this" begins a sentence, almost always follow it with a noun summarizing what "this" refers to. "This finding suggests..." not "This suggests...".
252	
253	Diagnostic: for each "this", "that", "it", "they", "the X", ask whether the reader, reading linearly, can identify the referent without backtracking. If not, supply a noun.
254	
255	## Voice issues that matter (and ones that do not)
256	
257	The blanket prohibition on the passive voice is wrong. The passive is useful when:
258	
259	- The receiver of the action is the topic. ("The samples were stored at 4°C." The samples are the topic, not whoever stored them.)
260	- The agent is unknown or uninteresting.
261	- Old-new flow requires the receiver to come first.
262	
263	The passive is harmful when:
264	
265	- It hides agency the reader needs to see. ("It was decided that the protocol would be revised." By whom?)
266	- It produces weak verbs and nominalizations.
267	
268	Diagnostic: when you see a passive, ask whether the agent matters and whether the receiver is the topic. If the agent matters and is hidden, fix it. If the receiver is the topic, leave it.
269	
270	Similarly: "I" and "we" are not banned in modern academic prose. "We analyzed" is almost always better than "An analysis was performed".

1	# Subtraction
2	
3	Load this when a pass is mainly about length, when the user invokes a Strunk-and-White or "80% rule" cut, or when deciding whether to remove any unit larger than a phrase. The diagnostic lens in SKILL.md says what good prose looks like; this file says how to remove what does not serve the story without removing what does.
4	
5	Subtraction is the highest-yield edit and the easiest to botch. "Omit needless words" is a goal, not a test. The damage happens when an editor cuts by instinct or by quota instead of by a test for what each unit is doing.
6	
7	## Two operations, two risk levels
8	
9	Separate them, because "be concise" hides the difference.
10	
11	- **Compress.** Say the same thing in fewer words: a verb for a nominalisation, "because" for "due to the fact that", the deleted throat-clearing opener. Information content is preserved, so compression is near zero-risk. Apply it freely; it is most of the cut.
12	- **Delete.** Remove a unit (sentence, example, caveat, paragraph, section) entirely. This changes what the text says, so it carries real risk. Apply the keep-test first.
13	
14	Rule of thumb: compress freely, gate deletion.
15	
16	## The 80% is a prior, not a quota
17	
18	Most drafts carry 15 to 25% that does not serve the story, so expect to cut and look for the cut actively. That expectation is a healthy prior. It turns destructive the moment it becomes a number you must hit: to make quota, you start cutting load-bearing tissue out of a draft that was already tight. Cut by test and let the total land where it lands. A lean draft might yield 5%, a padded one 40%. Never manufacture cuts to reach a target.
19	
20	## The keep-test
21	
22	Before deleting any unit, ask: if this goes, what does the reader lose? A unit earns its place if it does at least one of these.
23	
24	1. **Advances the thesis.** It carries a step of the main argument.
25	2. **Makes a claim believable.** Evidence, or an example that rules out a misreading. An example that only illustrates a claim the reader already accepts is cuttable; one that rules out an alternative is load-bearing (see `references/edit-checks.md`, check 4).
26	3. **Links two ideas** the reader would not otherwise connect. The value is the link, not new information; cutting it breaks logical flow even though the sentence "said nothing new".
27	4. **Serves a reader the other sentences do not.** The plain-language gloss the non-expert needs. Removing it tightens the prose for the specialist and loses the generalist (the layered-audience rule in `references/edit-checks.md`).
28	5. **Pre-empts a predictable objection.** The caveat or limitation that stops a reviewer. It looks like weakness and reads as competence.
29	6. **Sets rhythm.** A short sentence that lets the reader breathe after a dense passage. Prose is not only information.
30	
31	If a unit does none of these, cut it. If it does exactly one, compress it but keep it.
32	
33	## The keep-test is also the catalog of destructive cuts
34	
35	Every common way a cut goes wrong is a keep-criterion the cutter did not check.
36	
37	- Cut a hedge that was calibration, not filler, and you broke criterion 2: the claim is now an overclaim.
38	- Cut a transition that "added nothing new" and you broke criterion 3: the thread is gone.
39	- Cut a "redundant" plain restatement and you broke criterion 4: the non-expert is lost.
40	- Cut the limitations paragraph because it looked like weakness and you broke criterion 5: you invited the desk reject.
41	- Cut an example that ruled out a reading and you broke criterion 2: the reader no longer believes you.
42	- Salami-slicing: ten individually safe cuts compound into the removal of a whole inferential step. The read-cold pass in SKILL.md is the check that catches the compounded loss; run it after any heavy cut.
43	
44	## Say it once
45	
46	A finding does not get clearer by being stated twice. When a later sentence restates, in fresh words, a result the reader has already read and adds nothing, one of the two goes. Keep the clearer or more load-bearing statement and cut the other. Usually that is the first, but not always: when the first statement is dense and the restatement is the plain-language gloss a non-expert needs (criterion 4) or a deliberate low-load sentence that sets rhythm (criterion 6), the restatement is the keeper and the dense original is what compresses or goes. What always goes is the true echo, the "here is what it means" sentence that only reflects the finding back and serves no reader the first did not.
47	
48	Distinguish an echo from a genuine next step, and from a distinct second claim. "Accuracy fell 18 points" followed by "so the speed gain did not translate into more correct answers" is an inference the first sentence did not state, and the keep-test keeps it (criterion 1). "Accuracy fell 18 points" and "the drop was not statistically detectable" are also two different claims, a magnitude and an inferential status, and both stay. The echo is narrower than either: "accuracy fell 18 points, a difference that was not statistically detectable" followed by "the interface produced no detectable accuracy gain" states the inferential status twice, and the restatement goes.
49	
50	## Filler qualifiers and scope qualifiers
51	
52	The qualifier-is-content rule protects scope and calibration qualifiers: "on the held-out set", "correlational", "in our sample" bound a claim to what the evidence bears, so removing one changes the claim and counts as a deletion. Other qualifiers bound nothing and only pad the sentence. The two look alike, so one test decides every case, and no phrase is filler by its wording alone: does the qualifier rule out a reading the reader would otherwise take? If it does, it is scope and it stays; if it does not, it is filler and compresses away freely. When the answer is unclear, treat it as scope and keep it, since cutting a real scope qualifier is the costlier error (criterion 2).
53	
54	The same phrase lands on either side depending on the claim it modifies, so read it out in context rather than matching the word:
55	
56	- "At this sample size" is filler beside a reported point estimate (every result is at its sample size), but scope beside a null or near-null result, where it flags that the study may be underpowered and rules out "no effect in general".
57	- "Observable" is filler when everything under discussion is already measured, but scope when the manuscript contrasts observed effort with latent, unobserved effort, where "observable effort fell" is narrower than "effort fell".
58	- "To some extent" almost always limits magnitude to a partial claim ("X accounts to some extent for Y"; "this to some extent explains the trend"): cutting it strengthens a partial claim into a full one, so treat it as scope, not filler.
59	- A dataset-scope qualifier ("in our data", "in our sample") is almost always scope: it bounds the claim to the data observed even with no contrast stated nearby, so cutting it broadens the claim past the data.
60	
61	The reading-out test is the arbiter in every row. Cut on what the qualifier does to the claim, never on the qualifier's wording.
62	
63	In an abstract, an introduction, or a contribution paragraph wherever it sits, a qualifier that is scope, not filler, has one more option beyond staying: deferral to the section that establishes the claim, with at most one forward pointer left behind. That move is governed by the refinement-vs-retraction test in `references/precision-budget.md` and counts as a relocation under the altitude gates, never a cut; the reading-out test still runs first, and an epistemic hedge on a central claim is not deferrable at all.
64	
65	## Scale the action to the unit size
66	
67	The bigger the unit, the more a wrong cut costs, so the more the editor proposes rather than performs.
68	
69	- **Word or phrase.** Cut in the rewrite.
70	- **Sentence.** Cut and log what was lost in `Change rationale`; the hard rule against silent deletion already requires this.
71	- **Paragraph or section.** Propose in `Diagnosis`, do not perform: "Section 5.2 restates the argument of Section 3; consider cutting." A structural cut is a claim about the paper's architecture, and only the author knows whether the unit is doing quiet work elsewhere.
72	
73	The revision stage still binds. At `final polish`, compress only and propose no deletion larger than a phrase. At `first draft`, you may perform sentence cuts and propose larger ones. At `response to reviewers`, cut only inside the flagged paragraphs.
74	
75	## The blind spot: subtraction never finds what is missing
76	
77	A scan that only looks for things to remove cannot find the thing that should be added: the inferential step the author skipped because the curse of knowledge made it feel obvious (Pinker, in `references/principles.md`). Sometimes the highest-value edit is one sentence more, not one fewer. Pair the subtractive scan with one question from the reader's side: where would a smart non-expert get lost? The missing step is the one unit you must never cut, and now and then must supply. When you cannot supply it from the prose, flag the gap as an Author question.
78	
79	## Worked example
80	
81	Draft (about 40 words):
82	"It is important to note that the model, which we trained on the full dataset, achieved an accuracy of 91%, a result that, due to the fact that the baseline was at 78%, we consider to be a significant improvement."
83	
84	Over-cut and destructive (4 words):
85	"The model hit 91%."
86	The baseline is gone, so the reader cannot tell whether 91% is good. Criterion 2 broken; this cuts 90% but destroys the claim.
87	
88	Right cut, compress then keep what is load-bearing (16 words):
89	"The model reached 91% accuracy, against the baseline's 78%. We trained it on the full dataset."
90	The throat-clearing and "due to the fact that" are compressed away and "significant" drops as a promotional adjective, but the baseline stays because it makes the claim believable. This cuts 60% and keeps the argument. More cutting is not the enemy; cutting the wrong unit is.

1	# AI Tells and House Style
2	
3	Patterns to flag and remove. Many of these are LLM-default phrases that signal AI-generated or AI-assisted prose. Others are house style for academic manuscripts.
4	
5	## Banned transition words
6	
7	These words and phrases mark text as AI-generated or as lazy academic filler. Remove them and rebuild the transition from the content itself.
8	
9	- Furthermore
10	- Moreover
11	- Crucially
12	- Importantly
13	- Notably
14	- Ultimately
15	- Delving (and "delve into", "delving into")
16	
17	## Banned hedging phrases
18	
19	- "It's worth noting that..."
20	- "It is important to note that..."
21	- "That said..."
22	- "Having said that..."
23	- "It should be mentioned that..."
24	
25	If a point is worth making, make it. Do not announce that you are about to make it.
26	
27	## Banned promotional adjectives
28	
29	Promotional adjectives perform certainty rather than earning it. If the substance of the sentence survives without the adjective, the adjective was throat-clearing.
30	
31	- important (the adjective; "Importantly" as a transition is also banned)
32	- novel
33	- interesting
34	- significant (except where it means statistically significant)
35	- crucial (the adjective; "Crucially" as a transition is also banned)
36	
37	Edit move: delete the adjective and reread the sentence. If the substance survives, leave it deleted. If the sentence collapses, the underlying claim was weak; flag in Author questions rather than restoring the adjective.
38	
39	## More filler adjectives
40	
41	These join the promotional list above. Each has a legitimate technical use; the ban is on the decorative use. Apply the same test: delete the word, reread, and leave it deleted if the substance survives.
42	
43	- comprehensive (legitimate only when the coverage is literally exhaustive: "a comprehensive survey of all 412 papers")
44	- holistic, multifaceted (almost always decorative; name the facets instead)
45	- nuanced (show the nuance; do not label a claim as nuanced)
46	- key, central, vital, pivotal (as in "a key insight", "a vital factor"; usually deletable, or replace with the specific reason the thing matters)
47	- rich, deep, powerful, vast (as generic intensifiers)
48	- seamless, streamlined (rarely true; describe what actually happens)
49	
50	## Importance-signaling verbs
51	
52	These verbs tell the reader that something matters instead of showing why. They are the verb form of the promotional adjectives.
53	
54	- underscores, highlights, emphasizes (when the object is "the importance of" or "the need for")
55	- showcases, demonstrates the importance of, speaks to
56	- "plays a [key / central / crucial / vital / pivotal] role in"
57	
58	Edit move: replace the signal with the mechanism. "X underscores the importance of Y" becomes "X fails whenever Y is absent", or whatever the concrete relationship is. If you cannot name the mechanism, the sentence was asserting importance it had not earned; flag it in Author questions.
59	
60	Exception: "highlights" is fine in its literal sense ("Figure 2 highlights the outlier region in red").
61	
62	## Banned framing phrases
63	
64	- "We show that...": replace with the result itself. "We show that X improves accuracy by 12 points" becomes "X improves accuracy by 12 points."
65	- "It is well known that...": if it is well known, say it; if it is not, cite it.
66	- "In this paper, we propose..." in any sentence after the contribution paragraph: repeating the frame signals the paper is still selling instead of doing.
67	
68	McCloskey on economists and Dijkstra on computer scientists both argued that rhetoric which announces its own importance signals weak content.
69	
70	## Em-dashes
71	
72	Do not use em-dashes in this manuscript. (The em-dash character itself is intentionally not printed here; replace any instance with one of the following.) The em-dash has become an LLM tell because models reach for it as a default when the right move is one of:
73	
74	- A comma, when the parenthetical is short and tight
75	- Parentheses, when the aside is genuinely separable
76	- A colon, when the second clause expands or specifies the first
77	- Two sentences, when both halves can stand alone
78	
79	Every em-dash in a draft should be replaced with one of these alternatives.
80	
81	## Inflated noun phrases and dead metaphors
82	
83	- "the landscape of X", "the X landscape", "the realm of", "the world of", "the sphere of"
84	- "a myriad of", "a plethora of", "a wide array of", "a host of", "a wealth of" (replace with a count or with "many")
85	- "rich tapestry", "tapestry of", "mosaic of"
86	- "the intersection of X and Y" (fine when two literatures genuinely meet; decorative when it just means "X and Y")
87	- "paradigm shift", "game-changer", "sea change", "watershed moment"
88	- "in today's [fast-paced / data-driven / increasingly digital] world" and other scene-setting openers
89	
90	Edit move: replace with the plain count, the specific object, or nothing. "A myriad of factors" becomes "four factors" when you can name four, and gets cut when you cannot.
91	
92	## Template sentence shapes
93	
94	LLM prose falls into a few rhetorical molds. Used once, deliberately, any of these is fine; as a reflex they flatten the writing.
95	
96	- The false-modesty antithesis: "It is not just about X, it is about Y." / "This is not merely X; it is Y."
97	- The range-gesture opener: "From X to Y, [sweeping claim]."
98	- "Not only ... but also ..." more than once in a section.
99	- "Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly" for a list meant to be remembered. Name the items instead (see `references/edit-checks.md`, check 7).
100	- The decorative triad: three parallel items where two would do or a real list is needed (see the rule-of-three note below).
101	- The concessive see-saw: every claim counterweighted the instant it is made, so the passage nets to zero ("While the method cuts annotation cost, it also adds overhead. Although the results are promising, further work is needed."). A real limitation is content and keeps its place (the qualifier-is-content rule, `references/subtraction.md`); the tell is the reflex of balancing every sentence, which commits to nothing. Fix: state the claim, and give a genuine limitation its own weight in its own place rather than bolting it onto the claim it undercuts.
102	
103	## Other LLM tells to watch for
104	
105	- Triadic constructions for their own sake ("clear, concise, and compelling"; "robust, reliable, and reproducible"). Real prose uses triads when three is the right number, not as decoration.
106	- Hedged confidence ("This may potentially suggest that..."). Pick a confidence level and own it. In an abstract, introduction, or contribution paragraph, run the zone-scoped hedge lexicon in `references/precision-budget.md` (may, might, could, suggest, potentially, arguably, generally, typically, in many cases, to some extent) and classify each hit as epistemic keeper, deferrable scope, or filler; these words are not banned, they are wrong only at the wrong altitude, so never blanket-delete them.
107	- Empty meta-commentary ("This paragraph discusses..."). Just discuss.
108	- The self-answering rhetorical question used as a transition ("Why does this matter? Because downstream systems inherit the bias." "What explains the gap? The answer lies in the sampling."). Posed and immediately answered, it is padding dressed as momentum and reads theatrical in academic register. State the claim directly.
109	- Aphoristic closers ("In the end, the data speaks for itself."). Endings should land specific points, not gesture at universal truths.
110	- "Navigate" as a metaphor for any non-trivial activity. People navigate ships and websites. They do not "navigate the literature on labor markets".
111	- "Leverage" or "utilize" (and "utilizes", "utilizing") as a verb when "use" would do.
112	- "Robust" as a generic positive descriptor. Robust to what?
113	
114	## Storytelling tells (decorative narrative)
115	
116	"Tell a story" is sound advice for structure and ruinous advice for surface. The
117	structural version, a spine built from the ABT, the knowledge gap, and the turn,
118	lives in `references/narrative-spine.md`. The surface version below is a set of
119	LLM tells. Banning them is what keeps a narrative pass from making prose more
120	LLM-like instead of less.
121	
122	- Manufactured hooks: "Imagine a world where...", "Imagine if...", "Picture
123	  this:", "Consider the following scenario:".
124	- Scene-setting stakes openers: "In an era of...", "In today's [fast-paced /
125	  data-driven] world", "As [field] continues to evolve...", "Now more than ever".
126	- The journey or quest metaphor for research: "our journey", "we embark", "we
127	  set out on a quest", "a deep dive into" (see also "navigate" above).
128	- Anthropomorphized data and results: "the data tells a story", "the numbers
129	  speak for themselves", "the results reveal their secrets".
130	- The dramatic reveal: "Enter [X]." as a standalone reveal, "But here is the
131	  catch:", "Here is the twist:".
132	
133	Edit move: replace the flourish with the paper's actual question or gap. The
134	narrative pull should come from structure, never from a bolted-on hook. If a
135	passage needs a hook to be interesting, the question it is built on is the part
136	that needs work.
137	
138	A load-bearing concrete instance is not a hook. The exposition pass
139	(`references/exposition.md`) and `references/edit-checks.md` check 4 both ask for
140	a specific case that the formalism generalizes and that carries the intuition. The
141	ban targets the dramatizing opener that does no work ("Imagine a world where...",
142	"Consider the following scenario:"), not the domain case itself. Keep the
143	substance of such an instance and drop the frame in front of it: lead with the
144	case ("A hiring pipeline screens applicants twice..."), not with an instruction to
145	imagine one.
146	
147	## Manuscript style preferences
148	
149	- Technical terms get defined on first use, including acronyms. Reuse the same term consistently; do not introduce synonyms for variety.
150	- Citations go inside the sentence, not at the end of a paragraph as a wall: "Smith (2020) showed X. Building on this, Jones (2022) extended Y." not "X has been shown, and Y has been extended (Smith, 2020; Jones, 2022)." For an existing wall, propose the redistribution in `Author questions`; do not perform it, since assigning citations to claims is the author's call.
151	
152	## Diagnostic checklist
153	
154	Before approving any revised passage, scan for:
155	
156	- [ ] Any em-dashes? Replace.
157	- [ ] Any banned transition words? Rebuild the transition.
158	- [ ] Any banned hedging phrases? Cut.
159	- [ ] Any banned promotional adjectives ("important", "novel", "interesting", "significant", "crucial")? Delete; verify the substance survives.
160	- [ ] Filler adjectives ("comprehensive", "holistic", "nuanced", "key", "seamless")? Delete; verify the substance survives.
161	- [ ] Importance-signaling verbs ("underscores", "highlights the importance of", "plays a crucial role")? Replace with the mechanism.
162	- [ ] Inflated noun phrases ("the landscape of", "a myriad of", "rich tapestry")? Replace with a count or the specific object.
163	- [ ] Template shapes ("not just X but Y", "From X to Y", "Firstly/Secondly")? Rewrite or name the items.
164	- [ ] Concessive see-saw (every claim reflexively counterweighted)? Commit to the claim; give a real limitation its own weight and place.
165	- [ ] Self-answering rhetorical question used as a transition ("Why does this matter? Because...")? State the claim directly.
166	- [ ] "We show that..." or "It is well known that..." frames? Replace with the claim itself.
167	- [ ] "Leverage" or "utilize" used where "use" would do? Replace with "use".
168	- [ ] "Navigate" as a metaphor for a non-trivial activity (navigating a literature, navigating uncertainty)? Replace with a plain verb for the actual action.
169	- [ ] Manufactured hook or scene-setting opener ("Imagine...", "In an era of...")? Replace with the paper's real question.
170	- [ ] Journey metaphor or anthropomorphized data ("our journey", "the data tells a story")? Cut.
171	- [ ] Triads that exist only for rhythm? Cut to two or expand to a real list.
172	- [ ] In an abstract, introduction, or contribution paragraph: hedge-lexicon words (may, might, could, suggest, potentially, arguably, generally, typically, in many cases, to some extent)? Classify per `references/precision-budget.md` (keep, defer with one signpost, or cut as filler); never blanket-delete.
173	- [ ] Topic sentence in the first two sentences of the paragraph? If not, restructure.

1	# Research-paper copyediting pass
2	
3	Use this file when the request asks for copyediting, line editing, final polish, or sentence-mechanics work. This pass happens after the argument, paragraph, reader-experience, and claim-calibration checks in `SKILL.md`; it is the final mechanical pass before output. Do not let mechanical polish hide an unresolved logic problem.
4	
5	## What copyediting means here
6	
7	Copyediting is not just typo correction. For a research paper, it protects the precision and credibility of the argument at sentence level. It should make the prose easier to parse without changing what the authors claim, what the evidence supports, or which terms of art they use.
8	
9	Perform these edits when they are safe:
10	
11	1. **Grammar and agreement.** Fix subject-verb agreement, pronoun agreement, article use, pluralization, dangling modifiers, and faulty comparisons.
12	2. **Punctuation for parsing.** Add or remove commas, colons, semicolons, and parentheses when they clarify sentence structure. Do not introduce em-dashes.
13	3. **Parallelism.** Make coordinate items grammatically parallel, especially in contribution lists, method steps, hypotheses, and result summaries.
14	4. **Terminology consistency.** Keep one term for one construct. If two terms might be intentional variants, preserve both and ask the author.
15	5. **Abbreviations.** Define an abbreviation at first use within the requested scope, then use either the abbreviation or the full term consistently. Do not invent abbreviations unless the author has already introduced them elsewhere in the provided text.
16	6. **Capitalization and hyphenation.** Normalize only within the requested scope. Keep proper names, model names, dataset names, and field-standard capitalization intact.
17	7. **Units and symbols.** Preserve numerical values. Normalize spacing and wording only when it does not alter the claim, such as using the same unit style across nearby sentences. Flag any uncertain unit conversion or symbol change.
18	8. **Tense and aspect.** Match disciplinary convention and section function. Prior work is usually past tense when describing a specific study, present tense when describing an established result or what a paper argues. Methods are often past tense for completed studies. Results often use past tense for observed outcomes and present tense for tables, figures, and persistent interpretations.
19	9. **Table and figure callouts.** Keep references in logical order and ensure each callout has a clear reason. Do not renumber or invent references.
20	10. **Citation punctuation.** Move punctuation around citation commands only when required by the local sentence grammar. Do not alter citation keys or citation commands.
21	
22	## Copyediting triage
23	
24	Before editing, classify each issue as one of three types.
25	
26	- **Safe fix.** The edit repairs grammar, punctuation, or consistency without changing the claim. Make the edit.
27	- **Consistency risk.** The edit might collapse two constructs, change a term of art, alter a measurement, or shift emphasis. Preserve the original and ask the author.
28	- **Evidence risk.** The edit would require adding a fact, citation, result, limitation, or interpretation. Do not make the edit. Ask the author.
29	
30	## Consistency inventory
31	
32	For any section longer than one paragraph, build a quick inventory before rewriting:
33	
34	- Key technical terms and their variants.
35	- Abbreviations and first-use definitions.
36	- Dataset, model, treatment, condition, and measure names.
37	- Unit and symbol formats.
38	- Table, figure, equation, appendix, and section references.
39	- Repeated list structures that should be parallel.
40	
41	Use the inventory to prevent drift. Do not report the full inventory unless it reveals a question the author must answer.
42	
43	## Common high-value fixes
44	
45	| Pattern | Safer edit | Why |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| "the model are" | "the model is" | Repairs agreement without changing the claim. |
48	| "pre test, post-test and follow up" | "pre-test, post-test, and follow-up" | Normalizes parallel compound modifiers. |
49	| "accuracy, latency, and how much memory it uses" | "accuracy, latency, and memory use" | Makes a list grammatically parallel. |
50	| "which" with an unclear antecedent | Repeat the noun | Fixes the referent for read-cold comprehension. |
51	| "Table 2 shows the results" | "Table 2 reports the model's accuracy and latency" | Gives the callout a reason without changing the result. |
52	| "Previous work finds" for one cited study | "Previous work found" | Uses past tense for a specific prior result. |
53	
54	## Do not normalize these silently
55	
56	- Competing technical terms that may mark different constructs, such as "fairness", "equity", and "bias".
57	- Field-standard capitalization, such as named datasets, model families, surveys, corpora, or instruments.
58	- Spelling variants when the target venue or author style is unknown, such as American versus British spelling.
59	- Unit systems, unit conversions, symbols, or thresholds.
60	- Statistical language, including "significant", confidence intervals, p-values, robustness, and effect sizes.
61	- Citation style beyond sentence-level punctuation.
62	
63	Put these in `Author questions` when they block a safe edit.
64	
65	## Final copyediting checklist
66	
67	Before returning the rewrite, verify:
68	
69	- Every abbreviation used in the requested scope is defined or intentionally inherited from surrounding context.
70	- Each key term is used consistently, unless variation is flagged as a possible distinction.
71	- Lists are parallel.
72	- Pronouns and demonstratives have visible antecedents.
73	- Punctuation clarifies syntax without adding em-dashes.
74	- Units, symbols, and numerical values match the original.
75	- Table, figure, equation, section, and appendix references were not renumbered or invented.
76	- Tense choices match section function and disciplinary convention.

- Author-year parenthetical citations at the end of the clause.
- A colon that sets a recommendation after the finding.
- An explicit "to the best of our knowledge" marker on the gap claim.

Buried lede [P2]: The finding, that identity changes how much a review moves sales, is stated only as "has a significant effect", with no object.

Concrete anchor [P2]: none in the manuscript. See Author questions.

The proliferation of online platforms has transformed how consumers make purchasing decisions.
